full/data: Often the function to minimize is built from data: say fifty thousand photos, each a vector of numbers. Call how many there are N.
full/example: Each photo is called an example, and adds its own term to f: a number that depends on w and that one photo, small when w suits it. f is the average of the N terms.
full/per: So each example has its own gradient, the gradient of its term. These per-example gradients point roughly, but not exactly, the same way.
full/true: The slope of a sum is the sum of the slopes, so the gradient of f is the average of all N arrows. Call it the true gradient.
full/descent: Stepping w against it, downhill, step after step, is called gradient descent. But each exact step needs all fifty thousand gradients first.
full/poll: So do what a pollster does: ask a random few. Pick eight photos at random and average just their arrows. It lands close, for a sliver of the work.
full/B: How many you pick is the batch size, B. A batch is a group handled together, like a batch of loaves; this one is small next to N, so it is a minibatch.
average/per: Follow one entry of w. In a batch of four, say the examples' gradients for that entry are two, minus one, three and zero.
average/mean: The minibatch gradient is their average: they add up to four, and four over four is one.
average/used: Divide by B, the examples you used, not by N. The four stand in for all of them.
average/noise: Another batch gives another estimate: zero point two, then one point nine. Batch after batch, they scatter around the true gradient, here zero point eight.
average/more: Bigger batches scatter less: with more examples, more of their quirks cancel.
average/sqrt: The scatter shrinks like one over the square root of B, where the root sign means square root. So four times the batch halves the scatter.
average/cost: But every example in a batch needs its own gradient, so a step's work grows in proportion to B. Sixteen examples cost a quarter of what sixty four do.
average/trade: So small batches buy many cheap, noisy steps, and big ones fewer, steadier, costlier steps.
path/path: On the bowl from before, exact steps glide down to the bottom. Minibatch steps follow noisy estimates, so their path wobbles.
path/cancel: But each estimate points the true way on average, so the wobbles tend to cancel, and the path still closes in.
path/robbins: In 1951, Herbert Robbins and Sutton Monro proved this can work: a method that sees only noisy measurements, stepping after each one with shrinking steps, still homes in on the answer.
path/name: Their paper was called A Stochastic Approximation Method. Stochastic, from a Greek word for aiming, or guessing, means random.
path/sgd: So gradient descent on random examples is called stochastic gradient descent, or S G D. Strictly that means one example per step, but the name covers minibatches too.
epoch/shuffle: In practice, shuffle the examples, cut them into batches of B, and take the next batch each step. Here, twelve hundred examples in batches of a hundred.
epoch/epoch: One full pass through all N examples is called an epoch, an old word for a period of time.
epoch/count: Each step uses one batch, so an epoch takes N over B steps: twelve hundred over a hundred, twelve.
epoch/epochs: Three epochs take three times that: thirty six steps.
epoch/seen: After k steps, k times B examples have gone through. Five steps of a hundred: five hundred.
epoch/back: Turn that around to count epochs. Thirty six steps of a hundred are thirty six hundred examples.
epoch/div: Divide by N, twelve hundred: three epochs.
